analysis.one_liner: Sets a 30% minimum tax rate on income above $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add a new 'fair share tax' requiring taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $1 million to pay a minimum tax of 30% on the portion of their income above that threshold, after allowing for charitable deductions. The tax applies only to the amount by which the 30% minimum exceeds what they already pay in regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes. The $1 million threshold would rise with inflation after 2020. The bill also states the House's sense that Congress should close tax loopholes and simplify the tax code.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in two ways: the new tax is projected in the bill's own language to cut the federal deficit by billions of dollars a year, and it ensures that households earning more than $1 million a year pay at least a 30% effective rate rather than using deductions and lower capital-gains rates to pay proportionally less than middle-income earners.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 30% minimum tax on the excess of adjusted gross income over the $1 million threshold (after a charitable contribution deduction), so no household above that line pays a lower effective rate.
The tax phases in gradually based on how far a taxpayer's income is above $1 million, softening the hit at the threshold.
The bill's title and stated purpose are deficit reduction; its own text describes the tax as cutting the deficit by billions of dollars a year.
The $1 million threshold is indexed to inflation for years after 2020, keeping the tax aimed at the highest incomes rather than creeping down to middle earners.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income above $1 million a year — roughly the top 0.1% of filers — would owe more in years when their effective rate falls below 30%, typically because much of their income is capital gains or offset by deductions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied on adjusted gross income, so it reaches investment income and could push effective rates on capital gains to 30% for millionaires; opponents would argue this discourages saving and investment, though the actual behavioral effect is disputed.
It preserves charitable deductions as the one carve-out from the 30% floor, a concession that allows high-income givers to keep lowering their rate and that complicate the definition considerably.
A minimum tax on its own does not close the underlying loopholes; the bill itself frames this as only an 'interim step' until broader tax reform.
As a deficit-reduction measure it raises revenue without any accompanying spending commitment, so supporters cannot guarantee the revenue protects any particular program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's central tradeoff is modestly higher taxes on the top 0.1% of households in exchange for billions of dollars a year in deficit reduction, with no change to anyone under $1 million of income. The design is defensible — it phases in, indexes the threshold, and lets current tax payments (regular tax, AMT, payroll tax) count toward the 30% floor — but it is also explicitly a stopgap: the loopholes that let high earners pay low rates stay in place until broader reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2020 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2019 on July 30, 2020, joined by four Democratic cosponsors (Norton, Langevin, Khanna, and Pocan).
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to its Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a markup, floor vote, or hearing, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million a year keep their current lower effective rates, since the minimum tax was never enacted; no action was ever scheduled in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners keeping current low rates

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill died in committee without a roll call, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill would cap how low their effective tax rate can go, closing the gap that lets high earners pay proportionally less than many middle-income filers. Revenue raised would reduce the deficit borne by everyone else.
Because the 30% floor applies to adjusted gross income, it can reach capital gains, affecting the clients of private wealth and tax-advantage planners. The bill never advanced, so no effect was felt.
